title: The councils, again
hookLine: the Church thinks together over centuries
tomorrow: a rich kid, a runaway girl, a preacher, a letter-writer. who are they?

cards: Every family group chat has the thread that won't die: whose house for the holidays, who drives, who hosts. The first Christians had a bigger one.
Did people who weren't Jewish have to keep the whole law of Moses to follow Jesus? Acts says the argument got sharp. So the apostles and elders met in Jerusalem.
Peter spoke. Paul and Barnabas told what they'd seen. James weighed it all.
Then they sent a letter, and its key line, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, begins: "For it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us."

teach.b: Here's the question underneath: how does a community find the truth together? The Catholic answer starts in that room in Jerusalem. Not one genius with a vision.
Many people listening, arguing, praying, and trusting the Spirit is in the room with them.
That pattern became the councils: bishops gathered with the pope, from Nicaea, where the Creed took shape, all the way to the Second Vatican Council. The Church thinking out loud over centuries.
A neighbor tradition knows this ground well.
The Talmud records two great schools of Jewish teachers, the houses of Hillel and Shammai, arguing for a long time over how to keep the law.
Then, it says, a voice from heaven declared that both are the words of the living God, and the practice follows Hillel. Why Hillel?
Because his students were kind and humble, and taught their opponents' view, even stating it before their own. Shared ground: truth is sought together, with respect for the person across the table.

teach.h: KEPT ON THE PAGE, OR SETTLED.
teach.b: The Talmud keeps the losing side's arguments on the page, studied with care.
When a Catholic council defines a teaching, the Church receives it as binding for everyone, and the question is settled. Two families, both arguing for the sake of heaven.

how: Catholics profess the Creed shaped at the councils of Nicaea and Constantinople at Sunday Mass, and pray for Christian unity, especially during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity each January.

o: the private meetings where popes are chosen
the Church's bishops gathered to think together
the local groups that run a parish's money

p: the apostles and elders in Jerusalem
the council where the Creed took shape
both the words of the living God
that they all may be one

s: a council is one leader's private decision
it's many gathered; in Acts, apostles and elders together, with Peter, Paul, Barnabas and James speaking.
the Talmud keeps both Hillel's and Shammai's arguments
the practice follows Hillel, but Shammai's views stay on the page.
the letter in Acts 15 begins 'it seemed good to Peter'
it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us.

games.q: your parish is split on how to spend a big gift: a new roof or a food pantry. what would Acts 15 suggest first?
o: gather, hear each side, pray, then seek what seems good to all.
let the biggest donors decide, since it's their gift.
flip a coin so nobody's feelings get hurt.
games.why: in Acts 15 the apostles and elders listened to Peter, Paul, Barnabas and James, then wrote: it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind two people, in the Church or in your own family, who don't agree. Hold them both, without picking a side, for the whole sit.
If you pray, Jesus's own words in John's Gospel are there to borrow: that they all may be one.

wordCard.voice: The councils. Gatherings of the Church's bishops, from Jerusalem in Acts to Nicaea and beyond, thinking together.

orig.note: Latin: a council, a gathering called together.

carryVoice: Keep this: thinking together, the Holy Ghost and us, at one long table. Day done.
